- **Limitations:** It requires a disk-based storage system capable of handling many small files efficiently (mitigated by the directory hierarchy) [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the system requires a disk-based storage system capable of handling many small files efficiently, and that this is mitigated by a directory hierarchy. The evidence explicitly supports both parts: 1) It states that 'each leaf is saved in a separate file' and that the 'final number of files corresponding to the leaves of the octree may be large (e.g., tens of thousands)', implying a need to handle many small files. 2) It explicitly states that to avoid performance issues (linear search) with many files, 'we save the octree leaves in a hierarchy of directories, where each directory stores at most a certain number of files (typically 25)'. Thus, the directory hierarchy is the mitigation for the requirement of handling many small files.
supported

Unlike in-core brute-force approaches or algorithms that build from leaves upward, this method builds from the root downward, splitting leaves that exceed a primitive count limit, and ensures that each section insertion reads any affected node at most once [S1, unofficial].

The evidence supports all parts of the claim: 1) It explicitly contrasts the method with 'brute-force, in-core algorithm' and notes it differs from Cignoni et al. who 'build from leaves', whereas this algorithm 'builds the octree starting from the root' (downward). 2) It states the algorithm 'imposes a limit on the number of geometric primitives per leaf' and splits leaves that are 'full' (exceeding the limit). 3) It explicitly states that this algorithm 'reads an affected node at most once per section', unlike Ueng et al. which may read nodes multiple times.

Create $\lceil N/n \rceil$ sections of at most $n$ primitives each by reading at most $n$ primitives at a time and writing them to separate files [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the algorithm creates '$ceil(N/n)$' sections. However, the evidence explicitly states that the algorithm creates 'dN/ne' sections. In mathematical notation, 'dN/ne' corresponds to the ceiling function '$ceil(N/n)$'. Therefore, the claim is factually supported by the evidence.
supported
- **Bounding Box Growth:** If an incremental addition (new section) falls outside the original bounding box, the octree must be grown [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states: 'If we are building a dataset incrementally, a new section may not fit inside the bounding box of the original dataset. In this case... we grow the octree toward the new section. We create seven siblings for the current root node, and a new root that will be the parent of the old root and its new siblings.' This confirms that if a new section falls outside the original bounding box, the octree structure is grown (by adding siblings and a new root).
